Hammond Superintendent Cushman School Dear Sir, Please find the inclosed draft for $70.00. $40.00 is for Nora's fare both ways and expenses to come home and $30.00 for the girls to get clothes just to come home with. No doubt Carrie will get a pass as her term has expired. Respectfully Yours, Louis Pablo Box 292 Ronan Mont P.S. Excuse poor writing and expression. Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Jan. 16, 1919. Mrs. Louis Pablo, Ronan, Montana. My Dear Mrs. Pablo: I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of January 11, 1919. I inspect periodically the condition of the heads of the smaller children and require frequent reports from matrons as to the older girls; but girls as old as Nora are expected and required to comb their own heads. As I have just told Nora, it is no disgrace to have a head louse, but it is most disgraceful for a young lady to keep it. The matrons are required to inspect frequently and in case of need to make bountiful use of zapadilla seed, which soon puts an end of the pest. Nora was furnished with zapadilla seed and has been required to comb her hair. She has no bugs now, and I feel sure she has had none for some time. She does have a few nits which she is cleaning out. During the epidemic of Flu, the matrons and all employees were detailed as nurses consequently the little ones were not combed and bathed as frequently by the matron as during normal times. As soon as the ban was lifted, however, the pupils have received most careful attention and any found with head lice were immediately treated daily with zapadilla. A few still have some nits in their hair but these are being combed out as fast as possible. Regarding Nora's statement that she would lose her hair: I have just asked her whether the matron had threatened to cut her hair and she said "No, some of the girls said they would have their hair cut". No girl's hair is cut at this school unless by the Doctor's order in case of fever. I can't understand why Nora should have tried to give you the impression that she was neglected. She is given every opportunity and is required to keep herself clean. I have tried to make her realize that a young lady's first duty to herself is cleanliness. Thanking you very much for advising me of Nora's condition, I am, Sincerely yours, Superintendent Poulan, Mont. Jan 11, 1919. Mr. E.H. Hammond, Dear Sir - Nora writes, that she is just dirty with lice, and that they are going to shave her hair clean off. And she also writes me for some bug-medicine to clean her up. Now and I'm not going to send it to her for I did not send her down in such dirty condition, and I'm sure they can clean her up without spoiling her hair. But being that you're the Sup't I'm sure you should look into this and not only have Nora cleaned but inspect all the children and have them all cleaned, because I'm sure Nora did not bring such dirt down their, she must have got them from some- one else. Now Mr. Hammond I hope that you give this close attention and have this tended to right away, as I think it's an awful disgrace for Nora to be so dirty. Respectfully Yours, Mrs. Lewis Pablo, Ponan, Box 292 Mont. Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash., Nov. 5, 1918. Mrs. Louis Pablo, Ronan, Montana. Dear Madam: I have yours of November 1st. Nora is progressing very nicely towards complete recovery. Yesterday, her temperature was normal and if no complications arise, she will be as well as ever in a couple of weeks. Yours very truly, Superintendent BRH-S Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Nov. 5, 1918. Mrs. Louis Pablo, Ronan, Montana. Dear Madam: I have yours of November 1st. Nora is progressing very nicely towards complete recovery. Yesterday, her temperature was normal and if no complications arise, she will be as well as ever in a couple of weeks. Yours very truly, Superintendent ERR-S Pioneer Hotel Nov. 1, 1918 Mr. E.H. Hammond, Dear Sir - We thank you very much for letting us know about our daughter Nora. And would like for you to advise us right away if she should get any worse. Respectfully yours, Mr. & Mrs. L. Pahl. P.S. Would like to hear how Carrie is getting along, we haven't heard from her for some time, Dear Mr. Thero Pablo: Nora is progressing very nicely towards complete recovery. Yesterday, her temperature was normal and if no complications arise she will be as well as ever in a couple of weeks. Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Oct. 31, 1918. Mrs. Louis Pablo, Ronan, Montana. Dear Mrs. Pablo: Your daughter, Nora, was ill with the grippe and was to all appearances on the high road to complete recovery. She was however stricken with pneumonia and is still ill. Her sister, Carrie, is on the nursing detail and will assure you that we will do everything possible to help Nora to a speedy recovery. I have had a large number of pupils ill with the influenza but have been most fortunate in saving all except a comparatively few. Do not be unnecessarily alarmed. Nora will receive careful, expert nursing, and I will keep you advised from time to time as to her progress. Very sincerely yours, Superintendent Mr. Hammond: Nora Pablo has developed a temperature of 105.4° when she was found in the morning, and has a pain back and side. Mrs. Culbertson said to send her up to the hospital if need be but I do not know what to do. What do you suggest? C.E. Beers Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Jan. 22, 1920 Theodore Sharp, Supt. This form must be executed in duplicate when a child is transferred from a reservation to a nonreservation school. The Superintendent of the nonreservation school will retain the original for his files, and the duplicate shall be deposited in the reservation school records. The reservation superintendent should send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate as provided by law. All the blanks must be properly filled in every case. If the information called for on any part of the blank is not known, that fact should be stated. No space should be left unfilled. Whether the parent or the physician's name must be given. The person who signs the blank as consenting to the transfer should indicate his relation to the applicant by marking out the word "parent," "guardian," or "next of kin," leaving unmarked only the title appropriate to the signer. INDORSEMENTS. Applicable laws relating to the transfer of Indian children from reservations and schools are as follows: That hereafter no Indian child shall be sent from any Indian reservation to a school beyond the State or Territory in which said reservation is situated without the voluntary consent of the father or mother of such child if either of them are living, and if neither of them are living without the voluntary consent of the next of kin of such child. Such consent shall be made before the agent of the reservation, and he shall send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate that such consent has been voluntarily given before such child shall be removed from such reservation. And it shall be unlawful for any Indian agent or other employee of the Government to induce, or seek to induce, by withholding rations or by other improper means, the parents or next of kin of any Indian to consent to the removal of any Indian child beyond the limits of any reservation. (28 Stats., p. 906.) Provided, That hereafter no Indian child shall be taken from any school in any State or Territory to a school in any other State against its will or without the written consent of its parents. (29 Stats., p. 348.) That no Indian pupil under the age of fourteen years shall be transported at Government expense to any Indian school beyond the limits of the State or Territory in which the parents of such child reside or of the adjoining State or Territory. (35 Stat. L., 781.) The rules provide that— A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. An Indian boy or girl 18 years old and over may, without the consent of parents or others, personally sign the application form on its being changed to suit the case; but in all cases where the parents are living they should first be consulted. Compliance must be given to all orders and instructions promulgated in connection with the new course of study issued December 1, 1915. The information as to public school facilities called for in the certificate of the Superintendent (third page hereof) must be given, and all superintendents are especially directed to exhaust every means to secure enrollment of Indian children in the State public schools, pursuant to instructions heretofore issued in this regard.
